Ned Block's absent qualia objection deepens this problem. Imagine organizing a billion people to simulate a brain, each handling one neuron's function via walkie-talkie. Contemporary large language models fail multiple criteria that consciousness theories require. Chalmers identifies four obstacles: **lack of recurrent processing** (transformers are almost entirely feedforward), **no global workspace** (missing the limited-capacity workspace many theories require), **no unified agency** (these systems are "like chameleons that can take the shape of many different agents"), and **no persistent memory** (feedforward systems lack memory-like internal states persisting over time).

The model's vast knowledge exists frozen in weights; it cannot form new persistent memories or learn from experience beyond those weights. When a chat window closes, there is no persistence, no continuity, no memory of itself.
